extracted.intended_audience: complexity theorists, theoretical computer scientists, mathematicians, and informed readers evaluating claimed P vs. NP proofs
extracted.subtask_description: A short checklist-style guide for quickly deciding whether a claimed proof of P≠NP (or similar major complexity separations) is worth reading or likely to be correct, aimed at researchers and informed readers who need fast sanity checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge by author credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: The thing not to do is to worry about the author’s credentials or background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scott warns against dismissing or privileging a claim based on the author’s institutional affiliation or reputation: many historical mistakes came from such reasoning. Instead, use objective sanity checks on the manuscript itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanity check with easy variants (2SAT, XOR-SAT)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author can’t immediately explain why the proof fails for 2SAT, XOR-SAT, or other slight variants of NP-complete problems that are known to be in P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically this has been the single most important ‘sanity check’ for claimed proofs of P≠NP: many attempts are refuted by this test. If the approach does not immediately show why it does not (or cannot) separate known-in-P variants, this is a major red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof should “know about” known polynomial-time techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof doesn’t “know about” all known techniques for polynomial-time algorithms, including dynamic programming, linear and semidefinite programming, and holographic algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a stringent test related to the 2SAT/XOR-SAT check: a credible separation approach should explain why or how it accounts for known algorithmic techniques. Scott notes Mulmuley’s GCT as an example of an approach that aspires to ‘know about’ many nontrivial polynomial-time techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove weaker results along the way
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper doesn’t prove any weaker results along the way: for example, P≠PSPACE, NEXP⊄P/poly, NP⊄TC0, permanent not equivalent to determinant by linear projections, SAT requires superlinear time …
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P vs. NP is extraordinarily hard and should be thought of as many steps beyond current theorems; a plausible new approach should at least yield intermediate, weaker separations or progress on known difficult subproblems. Lack of any weaker consequences is suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encompass known lower bounds as special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Related to the previous sign, the proof doesn’t encompass the known lower bound results as special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask where, inside the argument, are the known lower bounds (e.g., against constant-depth circuits, Razborov’s monotone-circuit lower bounds, Raz’s lower bound against multilinear formulas). Since these are implied by P≠NP, a convincing proof should more-or-less explicitly imply them (at least in uniform versions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional lemma–theorem–proof structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper lacks the traditional lemma-theorem-proof structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impagliazzo pointed out that absence of the modular lemma/theorem/proof style is a warning sign: that structure helps isolate arguments and makes it much easier to find bugs (like modular programming). A paper that resists such structure is harder to verify and thus suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherent overview explaining how barriers are overcome
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper lacks a coherent overview, clearly explaining how and why it overcomes the barriers that foiled previous attempts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good overview should give a mental picture of how the proof works and why the known obstacles are avoided. Scott criticizes Deolalikar’s informal overview as opaque (comparing it to Heart of Darkness), and notes that inability to form a mental model is a negative sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on subtle descriptive-complexity issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof hinges on subtle issues in descriptive complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive-complexity arguments can be deceptive because small differences in encodings (e.g., presence/absence of an order relation) can correspond to huge complexity differences. Scott notes that heavy reliance on descriptive complexity has historically been a source of mistakes (and that this was one of the issues with Deolalikar’s attempt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overconfident tone / early grandiose claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Already in the first draft, the author waxes philosophical about the meaning of his accomplishment, profusely thanks those who made it possible, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An overconfident, celebratory tone in an early draft (e.g., “confirmations have already started arriving”) is a social/psychological red flag: it suggests the author may have underestimated the difficulty and not subjected the work to sufficient skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show how the proof evades known barriers (relativization/natural proofs/algebrization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A credible proof should explain how it overcomes the main known barriers to complexity separations (relativization, natural proofs, algebrization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters pointed out (and Scott acknowledged the omission) that one should explicitly address these standard barriers; demonstrating why the approach does not fall prey to them is a key part of convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physics/statistical-physics arguments — treat with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof apparently involved physics (statistical physics references) which can ring alarm bells because physics arguments are often less rigorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion is debated on the page: some commenters treat physics references as a red flag (physicists’ empiricism can be less rigorous), while Scott notes there is a well-established fruitful connection between random k-SAT and statistical physics and that physics insights have sometimes led to rigorous mathematical confirmations. Thus, physics involvement is neither definitive proof nor refutation but warrants careful scrutiny of how rigor is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post stable versions to arXiv (avoid moving target)
rubrics_metrics.description: If revising the paper, post versions to the arXiv so the paper won’t be a moving target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment by Greg Kuperberg: for the community to check and discuss, authors should upload versions publicly (e.g., arXiv) rather than continually changing an online manuscript; this aids reproducibility and review.
